title: Despair and the Bodisattva Vow
speaker: IkuShun Desiree Webster
summary: IkuShun Desiree Webster takes up despair and the bodhisattva vow as a tribute to Joanna Macy, reading from the "Despair Work" chapter of Macy's World as Lover, World as Self and a poem, "The Healing Time" by Pesha Gertler. IkuShun names IkuShun's own steps: acknowledging fear and sorrow, accepting the state of the planet, keeping joy alongside grief, and resting on the vow. IkuShun recalls Thich Nhat Hanh taking his monks and nuns to the ocean after 9/11, and a Jataka tale of the Buddha as a plumeria tree, which IkuShun's teacher answered with "you're a bodhisattva now." IkuShun closes with the Elm Dance, which Macy carried to grieving women in Novozybkov after Chernobyl, and gives the dance's basic steps.

sentences.text: Hi, good morning, everyone.
This is a re-recording from last night's talk after having some technical difficulties.
The title of this talk is Despair and the Bodhisattva Vow.
Dear friends, I'd like to continue with our tribute to Joanna Macy and her lifelong work.
I'd like to explore the topic of despair and how we work with despair as bodhisattvas in a world that's often difficult to navigate, through the tremendously muddy waters of our present time.
I also want to talk about another connected topic, grief, in the context of a story that I'd like to share at the end.
It's a story of her work that reconnects, and the organization she created, which empowers people to touch our grief and despair and also connect with each other by doing this together.
Before I forget, if you have an interest in her work and the organization, which I am thinking will still continue although she's passed away, you can look up Joanna Macy, the Work That Reconnects.
And at the end we're going to talk about the Elm Dance.
You can also look up Joanna Macy, the Elm Dance, and you'll find a lot of different YouTube videos on that.

For many years, since the first time I heard about Joanna Macy and her work in deep ecology and systems theory and ways for humans to reconnect, I have held her as a model for never giving up, for always continuing with her tireless action on the world's behalf and holding an optimistic outlook about possibilities.
I would think, how can she continue to do this?
How can she continue not to give up with each added bit of bad news about the state of the world, about injustices against human rights?
I would fear that she would give up, throw in the towel and just say, "I can't do this anymore."
I would ask myself the same questions about my root teacher, Thich Nhat Hanh, and about many bodhisattva role models in the world who seem to be unfazed, no matter what is thrown at them.
How could they continue to not be in despair when things are so unjust, when there is so much suffering and no fairy-tale endings, in truth, the reality of impermanence, illness and death?
As I've practiced over the years, I found support in these role models, the many mentors, teachers and friends, as well as support from the fruit of my own understanding as it develops.
This understanding has ripened for me over time, which has been fundamental in allowing me more freedom from getting lost in despair.
I'd like to explore that a little bit today.
Before I begin the discussion, though, I want to say right off the bat that it isn't that they've never experienced despair, or that they found a way to get rid of it.
It's important to see and acknowledge that we all have bouts of despair, being human in this topsy-turvy world.
The question is, how do we not stay in this state?
How do we experience it with acceptance and then not get lost in it?
It's taken me a lifetime to really explore my feelings of despair, of grief, of anger.
It's indeed a continuous practice.
It is the practice of awareness, the practice of recognizing avoidance.
In fact, the second chapter of Joanna Macy's famous book, World as Lover, World as Self, published in 1991, was entitled Despair Work.
It describes very clearly why it doesn't work to live in either despair or denial or avoidance.

It's quite easy, though, to understand why somebody falls into despair and why we often take the route of despair and avoidance as we encounter all the things that bring up so much pain or fear or anxiety or discomfort.
I'd like to read a couple of paragraphs from Joanna Macy's chapter on despair work from World as Lover, World as Self.
She says:
*Not surprising, we are feeling despair, we despair.
It is well merited by the machinery of mass death that we continue to create and serve.*
And now I think in the form of severe climate change.
*What is surprising is the extent to which we continue to hide this despair from ourselves and others.
Activists who try to arouse us to the fact that our survival is at stake, decry public apathy.
The cause of our apathy, however, is not mere indifference.
It stems from a fear of confronting the despair that lurks subliminally beneath the tenor of life as usual.
A dread of what's happening to our future stays on the fringes of awareness, too deep to name and too fearsome to face.
It's really kept at bay.
It's rarely acknowledged and expressed directly.
So the suppression of despair, like that of any recurrent response, produces a partial numbing of the psyche.
Expressions of anger or terror are muted, deadened as if a nerve had been cut.*
She goes on to say that the refusal to feel this takes a heavy toll.

*Not only is there an impoverishment of our emotional and sensory life, flowers are dimmer and less fragrant, our love's less ecstatic, but this psychic numbing also impedes our capacity to process and respond to information.
The energy expended in pushing down despair is diverted from more creative processes, depleting resilience and imagination that we really need for fresh visions and strategies.
Furthermore, the fear of despair can erect an invisible screen selectively filtering out anxiety-provoking data.
In a world where organisms require feedback to adapt and survive, this can be suicidal.*
*Despair is not banished by injections of optimism or sermons on positive thinking.
Like grief, it must be acknowledged and worked through.
This means it must be named and validated as a healthy, normal, human response to a situation we find ourselves in.
Faced and experienced, its power can be used as the frozen defenses of the psyche thaw, new energies are released.*
Joanna reminds us that despair work is different from grief work in that its aim is not acceptance of loss.
The loss hasn't already occurred, but it is similar in the dynamics unleashed by the willingness to acknowledge, feel and express inner pain.
I'll say more about grief work in a little bit.
The first step for me in my own despair work is acknowledging my own feelings, acknowledging the fear that is underlying my despair, and the anger that often wraps itself around it.
Acknowledging the sorrow too, and the despair of our times.

The second is acknowledging the reality of the state of our planet, the climate crisis, the mass extinction, and the fact that we as a human race appear to be underachieving what we are told are critical actions in terms of saving the planet as we know it, and the current life on it.
As Thich Nhat Hanh says, we must be able to acknowledge the possibility that this civilization may not make it, it may be destroyed.
We have to accept reality as it is.
The Diamond Sutra that cuts through illusion teaches us that we are greater than a single self, a single human being, a single lifetime.
If we include the vast history of even our own earth, we see that 100 years, 200 years, even 2,000 years is minuscule in terms of the geological history of our planet.
And the geological history of our planet is minuscule in terms of the history of our universe, and so on.
To accept this is to have freedom from our limited views.
It does not mean that we should not work towards allowing our planet and the forms that exist on it to experience less suffering.
It does mean that we touch a larger sense of reality, the ultimate dimension, at the same time.
So with despair, with grief, with sorrow, we feel and acknowledge first.
We can't move unless we move through.
We can't go around our despair.
It's important to name it and accept how things are in this very moment.
If things are hidden from our view by our own mind, they hinder our spirit more and more.
Here's a short poem from a book entitled The Wild Edge of Sorrow by Frances Weller.
This book was introduced to me by Aidan a couple days ago.
I have ordered it, but unfortunately I haven't read through the book before I gave the talk.
But I happened to find this poem, and it's short, so I'll read it to you.
It's called The Healing Time by Pesha Gertler.

*Finally, on my way to yes, I bump into all the places where I said no to my life, all the untended wounds and the red and purple scars, those hieroglyphs of pain carved into my skin and bones, those coded messages that sent me down the wrong street again and again, where I find them, the old wounds, the old misdirections, and I lift them one by one, close to my heart.
And I say, holy, holy.*
I'll read it one more time.

*Finally, on my way to yes, I bump into all the places where I said no to my life, all the untended wounds, the red and purple scars, those hieroglyphs of pain carved into my skin and bones, those coded messages that sent me down the wrong street again and again, where I find them, the old wounds, the old misdirections, and I lift them one by one, close to my heart.
And I say, holy, holy.*
We need acceptance and we also need joy.
This is a difficult task sometimes.
I think that we often feel guilty about having joy when we encounter great hardships in our community or read about the starving children in Gaza.
We feel that we shouldn't have joy when there's so much suffering.
However, my root teacher, Thich Nhat Hanh, taught me the necessity of holding joy along with our sorrow.
Joy is always present too, no matter how hard it may seem to find.

I remember that when 9/11 happened, the first thing Thay did was to gather up the monks and nuns and take them for a long walk down at the ocean to touch the joy of being alive, of being on this earth.
He knew that he and the many monks and nuns who had taken their bodhisattva vows could be of no use to others if they only dwelled in despair.
Lastly, I see how important it is, how it's been in my life, to have the bodhisattva vow as my ground.
I think that this vow I have taken, the bodhisattva vow, helps me not to sink into despair.
I am reminded of my vow to save all beings and energized by my bodhicitta, my aspiration to live for the benefit of all beings, my compassionate intention to liberate all beings from suffering.
I think what it does is allow me to touch my greater self, my Buddha nature, which is vast and capable of holding much more than my small self.
I remember a story that I heard several years ago when I practiced at Mountain Lamp.
It was one of the Jataka tales, stories about the previous lives of the Buddha.
It was recounting when the Buddha was a plumeria tree on the bank of a beautiful lotus pond.
In the story, a cunning heron lures creatures into the pond, assuring them that they're safe.
The heron then preys on them one by one.
The plumeria tree sees this with great sorrow, but it can't do anything to help them.
I was so saddened and very affected by this story, feeling the many times in my life where I encountered heartbreaking suffering and was unable to do anything to alleviate it.
I glumly told my teacher of the feeling and she immediately said, "Well, you're not a plumeria tree now, you're a bodhisattva."
This, of course, was the lesson of the story: the developing of great compassion and realizing the importance of strengthening one's intention to practice in order to develop an appropriate response.
So yes, I am a bodhisattva now.
This I am reminded of, and this is what guides my life.
So now, dear friends, I want to tell you the story of the Elm Dance.
I want to share this beautiful gift with you.
The music of the Elm Dance is a Latvian song, which became really popular at the time that the Latvian people were seeking to be free of Soviet rule.
It became a revolutionary song, a protest song with a double meaning in the lyrics.
People got to know this song, it was on the radio, more and more people knew it, and it really became a voice.
The choreographer who heard this song is German and wanted to choreograph a circle dance with it.
What she heard in the music and in the story of the song was that it carried the energy of intention.
She had studied the energetics of flowers and fragrances.
While the lyrics talk about oak trees and apple trees, the choreographer named it the Elm Dance because of the elm's energetic properties around intention.
It has been adapted.
It allows us to focus our energy.
During the second round, it has typically come to be that people speak out the names of those suffering, those being challenged, things that need our attention, human or non-human.
It also allows us to speak of our joy and connection with life as we hold each other in doing the circle dance.
Joanna Macy learned about the Elm Dance and brought it into her work with the Russian people.
She was leading workshops around Russia during the time in 1992.
She came to Novozybkov, where the highest rate of radiation was registering after the devastating Chernobyl incident.
Joanna didn't speak Russian or Ukrainian, so she wanted to share something to bring the people together, and she brought this dance.
What she and her cohorts found is that the people there were not ready to speak about the disaster of Chernobyl.
They did not even want to go there.
They did not even call it by name, referring to it as "the event."
Joanna was shocked to find at the retreat that the women there only wanted to talk about family relations, not about the event.

The Russian guide who brought Joanna and her cohort there had been talking over and over about the horror, the [unclear: "seeds"] of the radioactivity raining down on them, but they did not want to talk about it.
They began by remembering times before the event and how it used to be, and they did find some joy in this.
But then Joanna led them into a deep time exercise and they reached the year of 1986.
They all stopped and said, "We're not going back to that tragedy.
We are not going back."
By that very refusal to go back, they named the tragedy.
It all came pouring out with anger and tears, shouting, "Don't bring us there."
Then, oh, what happened is they started naming out loud one by one what had happened.
"Remember when this happened," or "when that happened," as they described the ash in the torrential rain, and that they figured out what was happening despite not having been told the truth.
And then the horrible illnesses after, and it all came out.
That evening, they turned on Joanna and said, "Look what you've done.
We were having such a nice time with those wonderful exercises.
Why have you done this to us?"
The very last person to speak stood up shouting, "I have two little girls.
Every time I look at them, I think of what tumors are growing in them.
Will my tears help with this?"
They had been doing the Elm Dance twice a day for the last couple of days, and they hadn't danced for years before that and they had yearned for dancing.
They loved that dance.
But now Joanna feared that they wouldn't come back for their last day.
She thought she had failed.
She thought that she had wrecked everything.
But then the next morning, every single person came back in their silence.
Joanna said, "It must have been so hard.
How was your night?"
The last woman who spoke up the night before said, "Yes, it was terrible.
I had a terrible night.
I cried all night.
But this morning, I feel different.
I feel that there's more room inside me.
When we dance and take each other's hands, we're like the trees swaying together in the wind.
That's how I'm feeling about these people in the retreat, now that we've talked about it."
On that last day of the retreat, Joanna said there was so much closeness with the retreatants.
They wanted copies of the Elm Dance.
They were making plans with each other, connecting and so alive.
Joanna said she fell in love with them.
She made a vow: "I will tell your story wherever I go, wherever I teach or share work."
She said she would say, "I've got a dance to share," and in that way she could tell their story.
The dance evolved and changed, and it really touched a global community over the years.
That's how I came to be introduced to the Elm Dance in the early 90s at a retreat in Boulder, Colorado, by a wonderful teacher, Katrina Reid, close to her.
It has remained very powerful in my heart.
Every time I hear it, it brings up such deep emotion.
When I heard of Joanna being in hospice, and being close to dying, I listened to the Elm Dance and it rekindled this deep love of things in me.
So I want to share it here tonight.
Actually, I wanted to share it last night, and we did do that.
It's easy to catch on to.
I played both the audio and the visual so that we could see it as a dance.
Because we already did this, and I'm re-recording, I will just briefly run through the instructions of the dance, but people can look it up if they'd like to.
You need plenty of room, a big room, wide enough for the circle of people.
Sometimes people would make an inner circle and an outer circle.
The dance consists of four beats of movement, alternating with four beats of swaying in place.
When swaying in place, imagine that you feel the energy of the earth and your heart spiraling up through the floor into your body.
When the energy reaches the heart chakra, send it out for the healing of the elms and for all beings.
This is the act of intention.
Anastasia Geng, who created the dance from the Latvian song, said the purpose of the dance is for building strong intention.
If people have an interest, like I said, they can look up the Elm Dance on YouTube and see how it works.
We had a really wonderful time revisiting that song.
I know a couple of people last night knew of it and knew of, or were very close to, Joanna Macy.
I really appreciate us being able to bring that alive again.
I think that's the end of this talk.
I appreciate everyone who was there last night and everyone who is listening to this re-recording.
Thank you so much.
